title: THE DARK REALITY OF CAPTCHAS · full film

beats.vo: Select all squares with traffic lights. Simple, right?

clip.plate: Luis von Ahn · CAPTCHA co-inventor · Wikimania 2015

beats.vo: He's right to apologize. We've all stared at that corner.
Researchers at UC Irvine added it up. Eight hundred nineteen million hours on reCAPTCHA alone. That's more than ninety thousand years.
beats.say: Researchers at UC Irvine added it up. Eight hundred nineteen million hours on re-CAPTCHA alone. That's more than ninety thousand years.

beats.vo: All that time didn't just vanish. Someone put it to work.
This is the dark reality of CAPTCHAs.
And by the end, you'll know exactly who cashed in.
It starts in the year two thousand, at Yahoo. Robots were signing up for millions of its free email accounts.
A first-year PhD student at Carnegie Mellon heard about it. His name was Luis von Ahn.
His idea was simple. A test any human can pass, and no computer can.
By two thousand three, it even had a name: CAPTCHA, short for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.
Then Luis did the math. Ten seconds a puzzle, two hundred million puzzles a day.
beats.say: Then Louis did the math. Ten seconds a puzzle, two hundred million puzzles a day.

beats.vo: That's sixty-three years of human time. Every single day.
So he asked a dangerous question. What if all that effort did real work?
And that's when the little box got a second job.
Look at the old two-word puzzles. One word was the test. The other came from a scanned book.
On older books, scanners missed about thirty percent of the words. Your eyes didn't.
Type the known word right, and your guess on the mystery word counts. When enough strangers agree, the book gets its word.
And it wasn't just books.
Even The New York Times sent its old archive through the box. About a year of newspapers, every four days.
Nobody signed up. Nobody got paid. Everybody thought they were just logging in.
In two thousand nine, Google bought reCAPTCHA. In its own words, to improve its book and newspaper scanning.
beats.say: In two thousand nine, Google bought re-CAPTCHA. In its own words, to improve its book and newspaper scanning.

beats.vo: Google never said what it paid. But look at what came with it.
And Luis? He ran the same play again. In twenty eleven, he co-founded Duolingo.
beats.say: And Louis? He ran the same play again. In twenty eleven, he co-founded Duolingo.

beats.vo: Learners translated real web articles. CNN and BuzzFeed paid for them.
Students thought they were practicing. They were translating the news.
And books were only the beginning. Next, they needed eyes on the street.

hero.plate: street view car · kowloonese · public domain

beats.vo: Meanwhile, all that free reading had a side effect. The computers were learning too.
In twenty fourteen, Google tested its hardest distorted text. Humans got it right thirty-three percent of the time. Its AI? Ninety-nine point eight.
So the words had to go. The first replacement came straight off the street. Blurry house numbers, shot by Google's Street View cars.

hero.plate: photo · infrogmation of new orleans · cc by 2.0

beats.vo: Then came pictures. Funny enough, that was the very first idea Luis had: show people a photo, and have them type what's in it.
beats.say: Then came pictures. Funny enough, that was the very first idea Louis had: show people a photo, and have them type what's in it.

beats.vo: It failed for a silly reason. People couldn't spell what they saw.
So this time, nobody types. You just click.
Buses. Crosswalks. Traffic lights. Fire hydrants. Ever notice they all look weirdly American?
Because they're street scenes. Exactly what a car's camera sees. And Google had launched Street View in two thousand seven.

R.plate: street view car · kowloonese · public domain

beats.vo: So every square you clicked became a label.
Now, the famous fire hydrant. Does that sliver of metal count? What about the base?
Same trick as the books. The edge is decided by votes. Where people hesitate, that's where the hydrant ends.

hero.plate: photo · infrogmation of new orleans · cc by 2.0

beats.vo: And then, the model went public. Your clicks became a product.
In twenty twenty, Cloudflare moved its CAPTCHAs from reCAPTCHA to a rival called hCaptcha.
beats.say: In twenty twenty, Cloudflare moved its CAPTCHAs from re-CAPTCHA to a rival called H-captcha.

beats.vo: Same puzzles. Same clicks. Just a new buyer.
Its pitch was blunt. Companies pay to get images labeled. Websites earn a cut for showing the puzzles. And you do the labeling.
So the puzzle you solve for free is a dataset someone else pays for.
Back in twenty fifteen, one user had already sued Google over the books. Her name was Gabriela Rojas-Lozano.

clip.plate: Sebastian Schmieg · on Rojas-Lozano v. Google · 34C3

beats.vo: In twenty sixteen, a judge threw the case out. A few seconds of typing, the court found, cost her nothing.
Cloudflare later did the math on all this clicking. Humanity wastes about five hundred years. Every single day. That's a full human lifetime, every four hours.
Meanwhile, the bots never really lost. They found a workaround. Humans.
Captcha-solving farms. Rows of real people, paid to solve puzzles for bots, all day long.
Picture the room. Rows of desks. Rows of screens. Buses and crosswalks, refreshing every few seconds. Nobody here is being tested. They're being paid.
Clicking for cents is a real job now. In Germany, researchers met people who click likes for a living.
The price? Starting at fifty cents per thousand images. That's a twentieth of a cent per puzzle.
For a few dollars, a bot can buy thousands of human answers.
A bot hits the box. It forwards the puzzle to a worker. They solve it in seconds. The bot walks right in.
So Google changed the game again. And this time, you can't even see the test.
Remember the famous checkbox? It launched in twenty fourteen. And the click was never the point.
It watches how you get there. How your mouse moves. Where it pauses. How long you hesitate.
Your hand wobbles on its way to the box. A cheap bot glides in a perfect straight line.
By twenty eighteen, Google was ready to drop the puzzle completely.
Google's own terms say it collects hardware and software information from your device. Put together, that's a fingerprint.
Here's the twist. Privacy can lower your score. A VPN. Fresh cookies. A blank browsing history. To the box, you start looking like a bot.
And when the system decides you're a robot, there's rarely an appeal button.
You just sit there, locked out, clicking the same squares again.
So. Remember the question from the start? Who cashed in?
Start with the UC Irvine study. It counted at least five hundred twelve billion reCAPTCHA sessions.
beats.say: Start with the UC Irvine study. It counted at least five hundred twelve billion re-CAPTCHA sessions.

beats.vo: Those eight hundred nineteen million hours? The same UC Irvine team put a price on them. About six point one billion dollars of free labor.
beats.say: Those eight hundred nineteen million hours? The same UC Irvine team put a price on them. About six point one billion dollars of free labor.

beats.vo: Their verdict? A tracking cookie farm for profit, masquerading as a security service.
Google says reCAPTCHA data isn't used for personalized ads. You decide who to believe.
Either way, you were never the customer. You were the product.
And the cruelest part? Bots now pass these tests better than we do. Sometimes every single time.
In 2024, researchers in Zurich built a bot that solved one hundred percent of the image puzzles.
beats.say: In twenty twenty-four, researchers in Zurich built a bot that solved one hundred percent of the image puzzles.

beats.vo: So the industry is quietly moving on. Invisible tokens. Device checks. Face scans. Even iris scanners.
Proving you're human may soon mean proving you are you.
And the man who started all of this? He thinks the ending is already written.
beats.say: And the man who started all of this? He thinks the ending is already written.

beats.vo: He believes computers will one day do everything humans can. And then no test will be able to tell us apart.
So look at that box one more time.
Two warped words. One little checkbox. A grid of blurry street corners.
For over twenty years, it asked one question. Are you a robot? And every answer made the robots a little more human.
The box was never just a test. It was a classroom.
You didn't fail the test. You trained the thing that passes it.
